claim: Education is related to a wide variety of beneficial health, behavioral, and societal outcomes.
source: Education is related to a wide variety of beneficial health, behavioral, and societal outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing these relationships.

claim: Individuals who experience more education tend to show a wide variety of beneficial health, cognitive, and neural outcomes.
source: Individuals who experience more education tend to show a wide variety of beneficial health, cognitive, and neural outcomes (Lövdén et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lövdén et al., 2020.

claim: Correlational evidence across disparate contexts, countries, and demographics offers overwhelming support for beneficial outcomes of education.
source: Correlational evidence across disparate contexts, countries, and demographics offers overwhelming support for these findings (Strand et al., 2010; Ross and Wu, 1996; Kobayashi et al., 2017; Waldstein et al., 2017; Livingston et al., 2020; Montez et al., 2012; Turrini et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Education increases learned skills and knowledge.
source: Education not only increases learned skills and knowledge, but also reasoning and fluid intelligence abilities (Ceci, 1991; Ritchie and Tucker-Drob, 2018; Means and Voss, 1996; Judd et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Education increases reasoning and fluid intelligence abilities.
source: Education not only increases learned skills and knowledge, but also reasoning and fluid intelligence abilities (Ceci, 1991; Ritchie and Tucker-Drob, 2018; Means and Voss, 1996; Judd et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Long-term reorganization of brain structure is one plausible mechanism underlying widespread benefits from education.
source: One plausible mechanism underlying these widespread benefits from education is the long-term reorganization of brain structure.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about a potential mechanism.

claim: Lifespan theories on heterogenous neurodevelopment place particular emphasis on education.
source: Lifespan theories on heterogenous neurodevelopment place particular emphasis on education (Cabeza et al., 2018; Buckner, 2004; Stern, 2002; Lindenberger and Lövdén, 2019; Newcombe, 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Correlative work supports the role of brain structure as a mechanism for education's benefits.
source: correlative work further supports the role of brain structure as a mechanism (Waldstein et al., 2017; Walhovd et al., 2022; Noble et al., 2012; Chan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to correlational studies.

claim: More educated individuals show higher mean cortical thickness in later life.
source: For instance, more educated individuals show higher mean cortical thickness (CT) in later life – taken as evidence of 'increased brain reserve' lessening the neurodegenerative effects of aging (Kim et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Higher cortical thickness in more educated individuals is taken as evidence of 'increased brain reserve' lessening the neurodegenerative effects of aging.
source: For instance, more educated individuals show higher mean cortical thickness (CT) in later life – taken as evidence of 'increased brain reserve' lessening the neurodegenerative effects of aging (Kim et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents an interpretation in the literature.

claim: Strong causal evidence for the effect of education on brain structure is severely lacking.
source: Yet, strong causal evidence for the effect of education on brain structure is severely lacking (Seyedsalehi et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review.

claim: Ethical and practical constraints mean that the effect of education cannot be experimentally tested.
source: Both ethical and practical constraints mean that the effect of education cannot be experimentally tested.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about research ethics and practical limitations.

claim: It is unclear if findings from education are causal or reflect a complex web of preexisting, interacting, sociodemographic and individual characteristics.
source: This makes it unclear if any findings from education are causal, or if instead, they reflect a complex web of preexisting, interacting, sociodemographic and individual characteristics (Lövdén et al., 2020; Hart et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations discussing confounding factors.

claim: Many sociodemographic and individual characteristics have been associated with brain structure.
source: many of which have been associated with brain structure (e.g. intelligence [Jung and Haier, 2007], parental income [Farah, 2017], neighborhood pollution [Bottenhorn et al., 2024]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is a substantial (~40% heritability) genetic component implicated in educational attainment.
source: Among the plethora of environmental factors, there is also a substantial (~40% heritability) genetic component implicated in educational attainment, further confounding potential effects (Branigan et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claim: Access to higher education involves substantial selection processes at the level of the individual and educational system.
source: In addition, access to higher education involves substantial selection processes at the level of the individual and educational system, which further complicate the causal pathways involved.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about educational systems.

claim: Natural experiments allow causal inference in observational phenomena.
source: One solution to this problem is using a natural experiment – a 'random-like' (exogenous) external event – allowing causal inference in observational phenomena (Lee and Lemieux, 2010; Cattaneo and Titiunik, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to methodological literature.

claim: A crucial feature of natural experiment design is an assignment mechanism outside a participant's control.
source: A crucial feature of this design is an assignment mechanism outside a participant's control, usually of natural (e.g. geographical, weather events) or governmental (e.g. policy decisions, cutoff rules) origin.
evidence: This claim is based on established methodological knowledge about natural experiments.

claim: A law that increases mandatory school years affects everyone equally, decoupling individual characteristics from the effects of additional education.
source: For instance, a law that increases the number of mandatory school years affects everyone equally, in turn, decoupling individual characteristics and other unmeasured confounders from the effects of additional education (Angrist and Krueger, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to methodological work and represents an inference about the design.

claim: Regression discontinuity is one of the most widely used causal inference analysis techniques.
source: One of the most widely used causal inference analysis techniques is regression discontinuity (RD), which is applicable when treatment is assigned via a cutoff of a particular score or running variable (Lee and Lemieux, 2010; Cattaneo and Titiunik, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to methodological literature.

claim: Recent advances in econometrics have optimized inference and largely standardized RD analysis.
source: Recent advances in the field of econometrics have optimized inference and largely standardized RD analysis (Cattaneo and Titiunik, 2022; Armstrong and Kolesár, 2018; Armstrong and Kolesár, 2020; Cattaneo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent methodological work.

claim: Natural experimental designs have provided robust evidence that additional education causes an increase in intelligence (0.14–0.35 SD).
source: Similar natural experimental designs have provided robust evidence that additional education causes an increase in intelligence (0.14–0.35 SD; Ritchie and Tucker-Drob, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a meta-analysis of natural experiments.

claim: Natural experiments have not been used to address questions in cognitive neuroscience.
source: Despite the many strengths and potential causal insights natural experiments offer the field of cognitive neuroscience, they have not been used to address such questions.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: On September 1, 1972, the minimum mandatory age to leave school was raised from 15 to 16 years of age in England, Scotland, and Wales.
source: On September 1 1972, the minimum mandatory age to leave school was raised from 15 to 16 years of age in England, Scotland, and Wales (called here 'ROSLA'; ROSLA, 1972).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the policy document.

claim: ROSLA resulted in almost 100% of children aged 15 staying in school for an additional year.
source: The consequence of this law change was substantial: it resulted in almost 100% of children aged 15 staying in school for an additional year, in turn, increasing formal qualifications, income, and cognition (Davies et al., 2018; Gorman, 2023; Clark and Royer, 2010; Clark and Royer, 2013; Barcellos et al., 2023; Barcellos et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on ROSLA.

claim: ROSLA increased formal qualifications, income, and cognition.
source: The consequence of this law change was substantial: it resulted in almost 100% of children aged 15 staying in school for an additional year, in turn, increasing formal qualifications, income, and cognition (Davies et al., 2018; Gorman, 2023; Clark and Royer, 2010; Clark and Royer, 2013; Barcellos et al., 2023; Barcellos et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on ROSLA.

claim: The UK BioBank has recruitment criteria matching the geographic and birth window of the natural experiment ROSLA.
source: One such cohort, the UK BioBank, has recruitment criteria matching the geographic and birth window of the natural experiment ROSLA (Alfaro-Almagro et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to UK Biobank documentation.

claim: The study used a preregistered design with over 30,000 participants.
source: Using a preregistered design (https://osf.io/rv38z/) with over 30,000 participants, we evaluate if an additional year of education, as mandated by ROSLA, causes changes in six global neural properties
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the preregistration and the study design.

claim: The study evaluated six global neural properties: total surface area, average cortical thickness, normalized total brain volume, mean weighted fractional anisotropy, white matter hyperintensities, and normalized cerebral spinal fluid volume.
source: we evaluate if an additional year of education, as mandated by ROSLA, causes changes in six global neural properties (total surface area [SA], average CT, normalized total brain volume [TBV], mean weighted fractional anisotropy [wFA], white matter hyperintensities [WMh], and normalized cerebral spinal fluid volume)
evidence: This claim describes the study design and outcomes measured.

claim: The study tested 66 individual cortical regions for surface area and cortical thickness.
source: For this reason, we further tested 66 individual cortical regions for SA and CT, 27 white matter fiber tracks for fractional anisotropy, and subcortical gray matter volume in 18 regions.
evidence: This claim describes the study design and regional analyses.

claim: The study tested 27 white matter fiber tracks for fractional anisotropy.
source: For this reason, we further tested 66 individual cortical regions for SA and CT, 27 white matter fiber tracks for fractional anisotropy, and subcortical gray matter volume in 18 regions.
evidence: This claim describes the study design and regional analyses.

claim: The study tested subcortical gray matter volume in 18 regions.
source: For this reason, we further tested 66 individual cortical regions for SA and CT, 27 white matter fiber tracks for fractional anisotropy, and subcortical gray matter volume in 18 regions.
evidence: This claim describes the study design and regional analyses.

claim: The study used fuzzy local-linear regression discontinuity analysis.
source: To test if an additional year of education causes long-lasting changes in neural properties, we used fuzzy local-linear RD (Armstrong and Kolesár, 2018; Armstrong and Kolesár, 2020).
evidence: This claim describes the analytical method used, supported by citations.

claim: ROSLA affected individuals based on a date of birth cutoff (September 1, 1957).
source: This continuity-based technique exploits the fact that ROSLA affected individuals based on a date of birth (DOB) cutoff (September 1, 1957).
evidence: This claim is based on the policy design.

claim: Adolescents born after September 1, 1957 had to spend one more year in school than those born one day earlier.
source: More specifically, adolescents born after this date had to spend one more year in school than those born only one day earlier.
evidence: This claim is based on the policy design.

claim: Compliance with ROSLA was very high (near 100%).
source: Compliance with ROSLA was very high (near 100%; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Most adolescents were continuing with education past 15 years of age before the policy change.
source: However, given the cultural and historical trends leading to an increase in school attendance before ROSLA, most adolescents were continuing with education past 15 years of age before the policy change (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Prior work has estimated that 25% of children would have left school a year earlier if not for ROSLA.
source: Prior work has estimated that 25% of children would have left school a year earlier if not for ROSLA (Clark and Royer, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Using the UK Biobank, the study estimates that approximately 10% of children would have left school a year earlier if not for ROSLA.
source: Using the UK Biobank, we estimate this proportion to be around 10%, as the sample is healthier and of higher SES than the general population (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 2; Fry et al., 2017; van Alten et al., 2024; Lyall et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The UK Biobank sample is healthier and of higher SES than the general population.
source: Using the UK Biobank, we estimate this proportion to be around 10%, as the sample is healthier and of higher SES than the general population (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 2; Fry et al., 2017; van Alten et al., 2024; Lyall et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on UK Biobank characteristics.

claim: The study used mean square error optimized bandwidths to a maximal range of 10 years before and after the cutoff (N>30,000).
source: To determine the optimal number of participants to include, we use mean square error optimized bandwidths to a maximal range of 10 years before and after the cutoff (N>30,000).
evidence: This claim describes the analytical approach used.

claim: The study observed no evidence of an effect from additional education on any preregistered global neuroimaging measures (p's>0.05).
source: Doing so, we observed no evidence of an effect from additional education on any of our preregistered global neuroimaging measures (p's>0.05; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis results reported in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The relationship between year of birth and neural outcomes was continuous around ROSLA's cutoff.
source: In other words, the relationship between the year of birth and neural outcomes was continuous around ROSLA's cutoff, indicating no differences in global structural measures from an extra year of education.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the statistical analysis results.

claim: The optimized bandwidths used in the analysis included participants born 20–35 months around the cutoff (average N=5124).
source: The optimized bandwidths used in this analysis included participants born 20–35 months around the cutoff (average N=5124).
evidence: This claim describes the analytical sample used.

claim: The absence of a causal effect of education was observed for all global neuroimaging metrics: total SA, average CT, normalized TBV, mean wFA, WMh, and normalized CSF volume.
source: The absence of a causal effect of education was observed for all our global neuroimaging metrics: total SA, average CT, normalized TBV, mean wFA, WMh, or normalized cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) volume (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The results did not change when imputing missing (~4%) covariate data.
source: These results did not change when imputing missing (~4%) covariate data.
evidence: This claim is based on robustness checks performed in the analysis.

claim: There was no evidence that individuals were able to adjust their enrollment around the ROSLA cutoff (Tq = –0.72, p=0.47).
source: However, for completeness, we tested this question (Cattaneo et al., 2018), finding no evidence that individuals were somehow able to adjust their enrollment (Tq = –0.72, p=0.47; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical test results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: None of the placebo outcomes (neuroimaging covariates) were related to ROSLA, except for one covariate (summer) which was deterministically related.
source: To accomplish this, we used all of our neuroimaging covariates (e.g. sex, head motion, site) as placebo outcomes, under the assumption that ROSLA should not affect these variables. Other than one covariate (summer), which was deterministically related to ROSLA (therefore excluded), none of the placebo outcomes were related to ROSLA (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by placebo outcome test results in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The findings add to existing body of prior work further solidifying ROSLA as a valid natural experiment.
source: Our findings add to the existing body of prior work (Davies et al., 2018; Clark and Royer, 2010; Clark and Royer, 2013; Barcellos et al., 2018) further solidifying ROSLA as a valid natural experiment.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the validation tests and prior literature.

claim: The study did not find an additional year of education to cause changes in any regions for cortical thickness or surface area (p'sFDR >0.05).
source: Despite these relatively high participant numbers, we did not find an additional year of education to cause changes in any regions for CT or SA (p'sFDR >0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis results.

claim: The regional analysis for cortical thickness included on average 5080 effective participants (N range = 3884–7771).
source: These analyses included on average 5080 effective participants (N range = 3884–7771) for CT and 5392 participants (N range = 3739–8727) for SA.
evidence: This claim describes the sample size for regional analyses.

claim: The regional analysis for surface area included on average 5392 participants (N range = 3739–8727).
source: These analyses included on average 5080 effective participants (N range = 3884–7771) for CT and 5392 participants (N range = 3739–8727) for SA.
evidence: This claim describes the sample size for regional analyses.

claim: Weighted mean fractional anisotropy in all 27 tracks tested was not affected by an additional year of education (p'sFDR >0.05; mean n=4766).
source: This was also the case for weighted mean fractional anisotropy in all 27 tracks tested (de Groot et al., 2013; p'sFDR >0.05; mean n=4766).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis results.

claim: The volume of 18 subcortical regions was not related to an additional year of education (p'sFDR > 0.05, mean n=5174).
source: Lastly, we tested the volume of 18 subcortical regions, finding none to be related to an additional year of education (p'sFDR > 0.05, mean n=5174).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis results.

claim: There was no evidence of an additional year of education affecting any regional neuroimaging measures with fuzzy local-linear RD.
source: To summarize, there was no evidence of an additional year of education affecting any regional neuroimaging measures with fuzzy local-linear RD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The study used local randomization framework as an additional preregistered robustness test.
source: As an additional preregistered robustness test, we used an alternate framework, often referred to as 'local randomization', to analyze natural experiments.
evidence: This claim describes the analytical approach used.

claim: Local randomization works under the assumption that individuals close to the cutoff are exchangeable and similar except for the treatment.
source: This approach works under the assumption that individuals close to the cutoff are exchangeable and similar except for the treatment (in our case an additional year of school; Cattaneo and Titiunik, 2022; Cattaneo et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is based on methodological knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The study compared participants born in August 1957 (n ≈ 130) to those born in September 1957 (n ≈ 100) for local randomization analysis.
source: To implement this analysis, we compared participants born exactly right before the cutoff (August 1957; n ≈ 130) to those born right after the cutoff (September 1957; n ≈ 100).
evidence: This claim describes the analytical sample used.

claim: The study implemented local randomization analysis in a Bayesian framework.
source: An additional benefit is that we implemented this analysis in a Bayesian framework, allowing us to more readily interpret the strength of evidence either in favor of the null or alternative hypothesis.
evidence: This claim describes the analytical approach used.

claim: The study observed strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for total SA (BF01=18.21) using local randomization with a normal prior (mean = 0, sd = 1).
source: Doing so, we replicated and extended our findings from fuzzy local-linear RD analysis, observing strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for total SA (BF01=18.21), average CT (BF01=15.09), TBV (BF01=13.61), wFA (BF01=11.63), WMh (BF01=13.26), and cerebral spinal fluid volume (BF01=14.50).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian analysis results.

claim: The study observed strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for average CT (BF01=15.09) using local randomization with a normal prior (mean = 0, sd = 1).
source: Doing so, we replicated and extended our findings from fuzzy local-linear RD analysis, observing strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for total SA (BF01=18.21), average CT (BF01=15.09), TBV (BF01=13.61), wFA (BF01=11.63), WMh (BF01=13.26), and cerebral spinal fluid volume (BF01=14.50).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian analysis results.

claim: The study observed strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for TBV (BF01=13.61) using local randomization with a normal prior (mean = 0, sd = 1).
source: Doing so, we replicated and extended our findings from fuzzy local-linear RD analysis, observing strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for total SA (BF01=18.21), average CT (BF01=15.09), TBV (BF01=13.61), wFA (BF01=11.63), WMh (BF01=13.26), and cerebral spinal fluid volume (BF01=14.50).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian analysis results.

claim: The study observed strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for wFA (BF01=11.63) using local randomization with a normal prior (mean = 0, sd = 1).
source: Doing so, we replicated and extended our findings from fuzzy local-linear RD analysis, observing strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for total SA (BF01=18.21), average CT (BF01=15.09), TBV (BF01=13.61), wFA (BF01=11.63), WMh (BF01=13.26), and cerebral spinal fluid volume (BF01=14.50).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian analysis results.

claim: The study observed strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for WMh (BF01=13.26) using local randomization with a normal prior (mean = 0, sd = 1).
source: Doing so, we replicated and extended our findings from fuzzy local-linear RD analysis, observing strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for total SA (BF01=18.21), average CT (BF01=15.09), TBV (BF01=13.61), wFA (BF01=11.63), WMh (BF01=13.26), and cerebral spinal fluid volume (BF01=14.50).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian analysis results.

claim: The study observed strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for cerebral spinal fluid volume (BF01=14.50) using local randomization with a normal prior (mean = 0, sd = 1).
source: Doing so, we replicated and extended our findings from fuzzy local-linear RD analysis, observing strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for total SA (BF01=18.21), average CT (BF01=15.09), TBV (BF01=13.61), wFA (BF01=11.63), WMh (BF01=13.26), and cerebral spinal fluid volume (BF01=14.50).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian analysis results.

claim: Testing across a range of priors did not meaningfully affect the inferences, as each showed evidence in favor of the null.
source: In addition, we tested across a range of priors which did not meaningfully affect our inferences, as each showed evidence in favor of the null (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Supplementary files 4 and 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary files 4 and 6.

claim: The study expanded the boundary to a 5-month window around September 1, 1957 (n per group ≈ 600) for local randomization analysis.
source: To examine the consequences of this tradeoff, we therefore expanded the boundary to a 5-month window around September 1, 1957 (n per group ≈ 600).
evidence: This claim describes the analytical approach used.

claim: The larger participant pool (5-month window) provided further evidence in support of the null hypothesis of education not affecting global neural measures.
source: This larger participant pool provided further evidence in support of the null hypothesis of education not affecting global neural measures (Figures 2 and 3, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2 and 3 and Supplementary file 6.

claim: Placebo outcome tests for both 1- and 5-month window local randomization analysis found no associations.
source: Lastly, we repeated our placebo outcome tests for both a 1- and 5-month window local randomization analysis, finding no associations (Supplementary file 5 and 7), demonstrating the robustness of the natural experiment ROSLA and our analysis approach.
evidence: This claim is supported by placebo outcome test results in Supplementary files 5 and 7.

claim: The UK Biobank is known to have 'healthy volunteer bias', as respondents tend to be healthier, more educated, and are more likely to own property.
source: The UK Biobank is known to have 'healthy volunteer bias', as respondents tend to be healthier, more educated, and are more likely to own property (Fry et al., 2017; van Alten et al., 2024; Lyall et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on UK Biobank characteristics.

claim: A benefit of natural experimental design is that it protects against threats to internal validity from selection bias.
source: One benefit of a natural experimental design is that it protects against threats to internal validity from selection bias (Barcellos et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is based on methodological knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The study estimates a 'local' average treatment effect for the subpopulation (UK, 1973, from 15 to 16 years of age, compliers).
source: Our results should be interpreted for this subpopulation (UK, 1973, from 15 to 16 years of age, compliers) as we estimate a 'local' average treatment effect (Choi and Lee, 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on methodological knowledge about RD designs supported by citation.

claim: Natural experimental designs offer the potential for high internal validity at the expense of external validity.
source: Natural experimental designs such as ours offer the potential for high internal validity at the expense of external validity.
evidence: This claim is based on methodological knowledge about natural experiments.

claim: The study reports a lack of causal evidence of a year of school on long-term neural outcomes in a large sample of aging individuals.
source: Here, we report a lack of causal evidence of a year of school on long-term neural outcomes in a large sample of aging individuals.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: The preregistered findings are robust across imaging modalities, different regions, and analysis strategies.
source: An additional year of education is a substantial intervention, and our preregistered findings are robust across imaging modalities, different regions, and analysis strategies.
evidence: This claim summarizes the robustness of the study findings.

claim: The results call into question sustained experience-dependent plasticity.
source: While our design cannot inform us of any short-term neural effects of education, our results call into question sustained experience-dependent plasticity, with significant ramifications for prominent theories of aging-related heterogeneity.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the null findings.

claim: The results have significant ramifications for prominent theories of aging-related heterogeneity.
source: While our design cannot inform us of any short-term neural effects of education, our results call into question sustained experience-dependent plasticity, with significant ramifications for prominent theories of aging-related heterogeneity.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the null findings.

claim: The recent availability of large neuroimaging cohort data paired with cutting-edge methods from econometrics offers new avenues in studying neural effects.
source: The recent availability of large neuroimaging cohort data paired with cutting-edge methods from econometrics offers new avenues in studying neural effects.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of recent developments in the field.

claim: Causal inference is a new tool to the neuroimager's toolkit with the potential to move the field of population neuroscience from association to causation.
source: Causal inference is a new tool to the neuroimager's toolkit – opening novel, societally relevant phenomena – with the potential to move the field of population neuroscience from one of association to one of causation.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge and speculation about the future of the field.

claim: In the correlational analysis using a 1-month window, five of six measures showed evidence in support of the null hypothesis.
source: First, we estimated the association between education (in years of attainment) and global neuroimaging measures using the same sample of participants from the one-month window local randomization analysis (i.e. August and September 1957; n~230). Similar to the causal approach, five of the six measures showed evidence in support of the null hypothesis (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian analysis results in Supplementary file 4.

claim: Total surface area showed weak evidence in support of a positive association with education (BF10=2.3, n=229) in the 1-month window correlational analysis.
source: In contrast, total SA showed weak evidence in support of a positive association of education (BF10=2.3, n=229).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian analysis results.

claim: The 5-month window correlational analysis provided strong evidence in support of a positive association between years of education and total SA (BF10=41.7, N=1185).
source: This considerably increased the strength of evidence in support of a positive association between years of education and total SA (BF10=41.7, N=1185).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian analysis results.

claim: The 5-month window correlational analysis provided extreme evidence in support of an association between years of education and cerebral spinal fluid volume (BF10=80.7, n=1193).
source: In addition, the larger pool of participants provided extreme evidence in support of an association between years of education and cerebral spinal fluid volume (BF10=80.7, n=1193).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian analysis results.

claim: The correlational analysis highlights the stark difference between a causal and associational approach.
source: This analysis highlights the stark difference between a causal and associational approach, while also providing evidence of sensitivity to brain-behavioral associations in the same sample.
evidence: This claim is an inference from comparing causal and correlational results.

claim: The correlational analysis provides evidence of sensitivity to brain-behavioral associations in the same sample.
source: This analysis highlights the stark difference between a causal and associational approach, while also providing evidence of sensitivity to brain-behavioral associations in the same sample.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the correlational results.

claim: A post hoc replication in eight additional 10-month cohorts indicates the preregistered report on the associational effect of educational attainment on CSF to be most likely a false positive.
source: A post hoc replication of this associational analysis in eight additional 10-month cohorts spaced 2 years apart (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) indicates our preregistered report on the associational effect of educational attainment on cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) to be most likely a false positive (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by replication analysis results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The positive association between surface area and educational attainment is robust across the additional eight replication cohorts.
source: Yet, the positive association between SA and educational attainment is robust across the additional eight replication cohorts.
evidence: This claim is supported by replication analysis results.

claim: The study finds converging evidence against a causal effect of education on long-term structural neuroimaging outcomes.
source: In a large, preregistered study, we find converging evidence against a causal effect of education on long-term structural neuroimaging outcomes.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: The null result is present across imaging modalities, different regions, and analysis strategies.
source: This null result is present across imaging modalities, different regions, and analysis strategies.
evidence: This claim summarizes the robustness of the null findings.

claim: The study finds no issues with the design of the 1972 ROSLA, substantiating it as a valid natural experiment.
source: We find no issues with the design of the 1972 ROSLA, substantiating it as a valid natural experiment, in agreement with prior work (Davies et al., 2018; Clark and Royer, 2010; Clark and Royer, 2013; Barcellos et al., 2023; Barcellos et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by validation tests and citations to prior work.

claim: Despite a large sample (min N=4238), the study finds no evidence of an effect of education on any global neuroimaging measures with continuity-based RD analysis.
source: Despite a large sample (min N=4238), we find no evidence of an effect of education on any of the global neuroimaging measures with a continuity-based RD analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis results.

claim: The study finds strong evidence in support of the null hypothesis for global neuroimaging measures using Bayesian local randomization analysis.
source: Confirming this result, we find strong evidence in support of the null hypothesis for these global neuroimaging measures using a Bayesian local randomization analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian analysis results.

claim: The study finds no regionally specific effect of education on local mean cortical thickness or surface area across 66 cortical regions.
source: Moreover, we find no regionally specific effect of education on local mean CTs or SA across 66 cortical regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by regional analysis results.

claim: The lack of localized effects was confirmed in weighted mean fractional anisotropy for 27 white matter tracks.
source: This lack of localized effects was further confirmed in weighted mean fractional anisotropy for 27 white matter tracks, as well as subcortical gray matter volume in 18 regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by regional analysis results.

claim: The lack of localized effects was confirmed in subcortical gray matter volume in 18 regions.
source: This lack of localized effects was further confirmed in weighted mean fractional anisotropy for 27 white matter tracks, as well as subcortical gray matter volume in 18 regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by regional analysis results.

claim: The study demonstrates the ability to find strong evidence in favor of observational associations between education and brain structure at this resolution.
source: Moreover, we demonstrate the ability to find strong evidence in favor of observational associations between education and brain structure at this resolution, suggesting our findings are not due to lack of sensitivity more generally.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlational analysis results.

claim: The robust null result is seemingly at odds with causal inference findings of education's positive behavioral effect on intelligence.
source: Our robust null result is seemingly at odds with causal inference findings of education's positive behavioral effect on intelligence (Ceci, 1991; Judd et al., 2022; Gorman, 2023) – which is sustained throughout decades (Ritchie and Tucker-Drob, 2018; Davies et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is an inference comparing the current findings to prior literature.

claim: The juxtaposition suggests that the neural manifestation of education's effect on cognitive abilities is at a level of resolution not detectable with conventional MRI field strengths.
source: This juxtaposition suggests that, to the extent that the additional year of education induced long-term changes in cognitive abilities, the neural manifestation is at a level of resolution not detectable with conventional MRI field strengths.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the null findings.

claim: High-intensity experimental behavioral interventions (e.g. juggling, studying, memory training) lead to measurable differences in brain structure in much smaller samples.
source: However, this would seem to contrast with a range of influential findings demonstrating that high-intensity experimental behavioral interventions (e.g. juggling, studying, memory training) lead to measurable differences in brain structure (with similar imaging pipelines) in much smaller samples (Draganski et al., 2006; Draganski et al., 2004; Bråthen et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: A year of education is an extensive period of learning compared to high-intensity interventions.
source: Moreover, compared to even these high-intensity interventions, a year of education is an extensive period of learning.
evidence: This claim is based on logical comparison.

claim: The 1972 ROSLA was well implemented, schools had time to prepare and were given additional funding.
source: The 1972 ROSLA was well implemented, schools had time to prepare and were given additional funding, increasing standardized formal qualifications of those affected (Clark and Royer, 2013; Barcellos et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on ROSLA implementation.

claim: ROSLA increased standardized formal qualifications of those affected.
source: The 1972 ROSLA was well implemented, schools had time to prepare and were given additional funding, increasing standardized formal qualifications of those affected (Clark and Royer, 2013; Barcellos et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on ROSLA effects.

claim: Expansion-renormalization posits that following a period of skill acquisition, the cortex initially expands and then renormalizes over the course of a few months.
source: One potential explanation to account for this discrepancy is the concept of expansion-renormalization (Wenger et al., 2017; Garzón et al., 2023), which posits that following a period of skill acquisition, the cortex initially expands and then renormalizes over the course of a few months.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: MRI effects at the macro-scale might have been detectable immediately post-ROSLA in 16-year-old adolescents, before renormalizing to a micro-scale.
source: In our context, this would suggest that the additional year would have manifested at a level detectable in MRI when the difference in educational exposure between children pre- and post-ROSLA was most pronounced and recent. In other words, MRI effects at the macro-scale might have been detectable immediately post-ROSLA in 16-year-old adolescents, before renormalizing to a micro-scale, leaving in place permanent, but microstructural changes (Hille et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the expansion-renormalization theory.

claim: Possible cellular candidates for initial experience-dependent plasticity are an increase in dendritic spines, the swelling of astrocytes, and intracortical myelin adaptations.
source: Possible cellular candidates for initial experience-dependent plasticity are an increase in dendritic spines, the swelling of astrocytes, and intracortical myelin adaptations (Hille et al., 2024; Mediavilla et al., 2022; Schmidt et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to cellular neuroscience literature.

claim: These structural changes may be detectable using other approaches such as in vivo cellular work, extreme high field strengths, or postmortem histology.
source: These structural changes may be detectable using other approaches such as in vivo cellular work (cf. Goriounova et al., 2018), extreme high field strengths (Garzón et al., 2023; Vachha and Huang, 2021), or postmortem histology (Perneczky et al., 2009; López-Otín et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential future research approaches, supported by citations.

claim: The long period of time (46 years) between additional education and neuroimaging offers both strengths and weaknesses for the study design.
source: Additionally, the long period of time between additional education and neuroimaging offers both strengths and weaknesses for our design.
evidence: This is an inference about the study design.

claim: It could be the case that 46 years is too long and any potential effect faded out over the years.
source: First, it could be the case that 46 years is too long and any potential effect faded out over the years.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the null findings.

claim: Prominent aging-related theories argue that life course experiences offer a reserve or 'brain buffer' that leads to an increasing cascade of processes limiting adverse aging effects.
source: However, we note that prominent aging-related theories of heterogeneity argue directly against this rationale, instead positing life course experiences offer a reserve or 'brain buffer' that leads to an increasing cascade of processes limiting adverse aging effects (Cabeza et al., 2018; Buckner, 2004; Stern, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: The timing between the intervention (ROSLA) and scanning makes the study design particularly well-powered to test aging-related theories.
source: Here, the timing between our intervention (ROSLA) and scanning makes our design particularly well-powered to test these theories, since education would contribute to an initial brain buffer (intercept) and any cumulative educational effect (slope) over 46 years.
evidence: This is an inference about the study design's strengths.

claim: A recent longitudinal study found prior education to not affect the rate of brain aging.
source: While our results are at odds with prior conceptual and observational work, a recent longitudinal study found prior education to not affect the rate of brain aging (Nyberg et al., 2021) – in alignment with our findings.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a longitudinal study.

claim: The correlational analysis found evidence to support an association between more years of education and greater surface area and cerebral spinal fluid volume.
source: We found evidence to support an association between more years of education and greater SA and cerebral spinal fluid volume.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlational analysis results.

claim: The correlational result emphasizes the need for caution in attributing causation in non-causal designs.
source: This result emphasizes the need for caution in attributing causation in non-causal designs, as unobserved confounders can masquerade as an effect of interest.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing causal and correlational results.

claim: More education is frequently highlighted as offering behavioral and neural protection against the adverse effects of aging.
source: For instance, more education is frequently highlighted as offering behavioral and neural protection against the adverse effects of aging (Cabeza et al., 2018; Buckner, 2004; Stern, 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: While the study replicates the inference associationally, it finds no causal evidence for any neuroprotective effects of education.
source: while we replicate this inference associationally, we find no causal evidence for any neuroprotective effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing causal and correlational results.

claim: The findings suggest a more complex pathway of effects unfolding over time.
source: This suggests a more complex pathway of effects unfolding over time.
evidence: This is an inference from the discrepancy between causal and correlational findings.

claim: Environmental causes are most likely very small and additive, which makes them difficult to study and hard to adequately control.
source: Environmental causes are most likely very small and additive, which makes them not only difficult to study (Burt and Johnson, 2023) but also equally hard to adequately control (von Stumm and d'Apice, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to methodological literature.

claim: To truly understand the neural and behavioral processes after interventions such as education, a multipronged, mixed methods approach is needed.
source: Our findings suggest that to truly understand the neural and behavioral processes that unfold after interventions such as education, we need a multipronged, mixed methods approach that combines deep phenotyping, longitudinal imaging, and behavioral follow-up (Pfeifer et al., 2018; Molenaar, 2004; Schwartz and Glymour, 2023), as well as more sophisticated models that can capture gene-by-environment interplay (Judd et al., 2022; Burt and Johnson, 2023; Dolan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative recommendation based on the findings, supported by citations.

claim: UK Biobank respondents tend to be healthier, more educated, and are more likely to own property.
source: The UK Biobank is known to have 'healthy volunteer bias', as respondents tend to be healthier, more educated, and are more likely to own property (Fry et al., 2017; van Alten et al., 2024; Lyall et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on UK Biobank characteristics.

claim: One benefit of natural experimental design is that it protects against threats to internal validity from selection bias.
source: One benefit of a natural experimental design is that it protects against threats to internal validity from selection bias (Barcellos et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is based on methodological knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A more pressing limitation is the study's power to detect effects using a sample of higher-educated individuals.
source: A more pressing limitation – in particular, for an education policy change – is our power to detect effects using a sample of higher-educated individuals.
evidence: This is an inference about a limitation of the study.

claim: The study estimates the percentage of 15-year-olds impacted by ROSLA to be 10% in neuro-UKB.
source: This is evident in our first stage analysis examining the percentage of 15-year-olds impacted by ROSLA, which we estimate to be 10% in neuro-UKB (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The percentage of 15-year-olds impacted by ROSLA has been reported to be 25% in the UK general population.
source: yet has been reported to be 25% in the UK general population (Clark and Royer, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The results should be interpreted for the subpopulation (UK, 1973, from 15 to 16 years of age, compliers) as the study estimates a 'local' average treatment effect.
source: Our results should be interpreted for this subpopulation (UK, 1973, from 15 to 16 years of age, compliers) as we estimate a 'local' average treatment effect (Choi and Lee, 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on methodological knowledge about RD designs supported by citation.

claim: Natural experimental designs offer the potential for high internal validity at the expense of external validity.
source: Natural experimental designs such as ours offer the potential for high internal validity at the expense of external validity.
evidence: This claim is based on methodological knowledge about natural experiments.

claim: The study reports a lack of causal evidence of a year of school on long-term neural outcomes in a large sample of aging individuals.
source: Here, we report a lack of causal evidence of a year of school on long-term neural outcomes in a large sample of aging individuals.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: The results call into question sustained experience-dependent plasticity.
source: While our design cannot inform us of any short-term neural effects of education, our results call into question sustained experience-dependent plasticity, with significant ramifications for prominent theories of aging-related heterogeneity.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the null findings.

claim: Causal inference is a new tool to the neuroimager's toolkit with the potential to move the field of population neuroscience from association to causation.
source: Causal inference is a new tool to the neuroimager's toolkit – opening novel, societally relevant phenomena – with the potential to move the field of population neuroscience from one of association to one of causation.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge and speculation about the future of the field.
